# Total and Composite Training Objectives


## Overview
Total and Composite Training Objectives aggregate multiple supervision signals into a single scalar value for optimizing [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) representations [G]. They solve the problem of balancing photometric fidelity, geometric consistency, semantic alignment, and regularization constraints during end-to-end training [G]. What sets this family apart from its siblings is that it serves as the structural definition for how individual loss components are combined, weighted, and scheduled, rather than defining the specific metric for a single signal [G].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism of all methods in this family is the weighted summation of individual loss components $\mathcal{L}_k$ to form a total loss $L_{tot}$ [G]:
$$ L_{tot} = \sum_{k} \lambda_k \mathcal{L}_k $$
Where:
*   $\mathcal{L}_k$ represents a specific loss term (e.g., photometric, geometric, semantic, regularization) [G].
*   $\lambda_k$ is a scalar hyperparameter controlling the contribution of term $k$ [G].

The specific instantiation of this formula varies based on the representation (e.g., [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md), Voxel Grids, Implicit Neural Fields), the training stage (e.g., initialization, refinement, dynamic growth), and the scale of supervision [G]. The components $\mathcal{L}_k$ are computed per-pixel or per-voxel and then aggregated (summed or averaged) before weighting [G].

## Subtopics

### [Overall Training Loss](10621-overall-training-loss.md)
The [overall training loss](#10621-overall-training-loss.md) aggregates multiple supervision signals into a single scalar value for optimizing differentiable volume rendering representations. It serves as the final aggregation layer in the optimization procedure, weighting components according to the chosen representation and training stage. Choose this method when end-to-end training requires balancing photometric, geometric, and semantic constraints across varying representations.

### [Multi-scale Joint Training Loss](13064-multi-scale-joint-training-loss.md)
[Multi-scale joint training loss](#13064-multi-scale-joint-training-loss.md) balances low-frequency structural consistency with high-frequency detail fidelity by simultaneously optimizing outputs from multiple network stages or scales. Choose this method during iterative refinement or dynamic network growth to address noise interference and detail loss.

### [Total Loss Function for Neural Scene Reconstruction](15309-total-loss-function-for-neural-scene-reconstruction.md)
This method defines the composite objective function used to optimize neural scene reconstruction models, specifically those utilizing Signed Radial Distance Functions (SRDF) or similar implicit representations. It distinguishes itself by explicitly including 2.5D geometric supervision (depth and normals) and 3D visibility priors to resolve training instability and geometric ambiguity. Choose this method when direct 3D geometric constraints are needed beyond image-space consistency.

### [Joint Training Losses](16752-joint-training-losses.md)
This method defines a composite objective function for the joint optimization of a [Template-Free NeRF (TFS-NeRF)](#16781-template-free-nerf-tfs-nerf.md), an Implicit Neural Network (INN) for spatial transformation, and a skinning weight prediction network. It distinguishes itself by explicitly constraining the INN and skinning networks through pose, cycle consistency, and skinning weight losses. Choose this method for dynamic scene reconstruction to resolve ambiguities in canonical points and skinning weights.

## Background
The concept of composite training objectives in [neural rendering](#6800-neural-rendering.md) evolved from the need to stabilize the training of [implicit neural representations](#19545-implicit-neural-representation-inr.md) and explicit Gaussian splats, which are often under-constrained by photometric data alone [G]. Early works introduced geometric priors (depth, normals) into the loss function to guide [SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) learning [G]. As methods diversified into Gaussian Splatting and dynamic scene reconstruction, the loss formulation expanded to include semantic consistency, cycle consistency for deformation, and multi-scale refinement terms [G]. The current family of objectives reflects a modular approach, allowing researchers to mix and match photometric, geometric, semantic, and regularization terms based on the specific requirements of the scene representation and available supervision signals [G].
